title: Final Devoicing
subtitle: Why German words end crisp — b→p, d→t, g→k.
objectives: Recognize and produce final devoicing automatically.
Distinguish pairs like lieb/lieben, Kind/Kinder, Tag/Tage by sound.
Understand that spelling does not change, but pronunciation does.

sections.heading: The crispness of German
sections.body:
German voices b, d, g when they appear inside a word between vowels. But at the end of a word, or at the end of a syllable before a consonant, they devoice. B becomes [p], d becomes [t], g becomes [k]. The spelling does not change. The sound does.

This is called *Auslautverhärtung* — final-sound hardening. It is one of the signatures of German phonology. It makes German endings sound sharp and distinct.

sections.heading: The three devoicing pairs
sections.body:
B / P:
  lieben (to love) — lee-ben [b]
  lieb (dear) — leep [p]

D / T:
  Kinder (children) — kin-der [d]
  Kind (child) — kint [t]

G / K:
  Tage (days) — tah-guh [g]
  Tag (day) — tahk [k]

The letter does not change. B stays written as b. But your mouth says [p].

sections.heading: When devoicing happens
sections.body:
Devoicing occurs:

  1. At the end of a word: Rad (wheel) = raht.
  2. At the end of a syllable before another consonant: Radfahrer (cyclist) = raht-fah-rer.
  3. Before a suffix that starts with a consonant: liebst (you love) = leepst.

Devoicing does NOT occur:

  1. Between two vowels: Leben (life) = lay-ben [b].
  2. Before a suffix that starts with a vowel: lieben = lee-ben [b].

The rule is mechanical. Learn it once; apply it everywhere.

sections.heading: Examples from Goethe
sections.body:
"Über allen Gipfeln ist Ruh." (Over all peaks is rest.)

  Gipfeln — the -n keeps the [f] voiced? No. The p is voiceless already. But notice ist: spelled with t, sounds like [t]. No change needed.
  Ruh — final h is silent, so this is just Ru, and the u is the end of the word. No devoicing here; no voiced consonant to devoice.

Better example: "Ein Wort, ein Satz" (A word, a sentence).

  Wort — ends in t, pronounced [t]. No devoicing; t is already voiceless.
  Satz — ends in tz [ts]. No devoicing.

Better still: "Ich hab es getragen" (I have borne it).

  hab — from *haben*. Final b devoices to [p]: hahp.
  getragen — the g in *ge-* is internal, stays [g]. The final *-en* keeps the g of *trag-* internal too, so it stays [g]: guh-trah-gen.

But: "Was ich trag" (what I bear).

  trag — final g devoices to [k]: trahk.

sections.heading: Listening drill — voiced vs. devoiced
sections.instructions: Each pair is read twice. Listen for the devoicing at the end of the first word. Repeat both.

items.answer: A phonological rule in German where b, d, g become [p], [t], [k] at the end of a word or syllable.

items.prompt: Does the spelling change when a consonant devoices?
items.answer: No. The spelling stays the same. Only the pronunciation changes.
Between two vowels, or before a suffix that starts with a vowel. Lieben keeps the [b] because the b is followed by -en.

sections.heading: Words demonstrating devoicing
sections.instructions: Read each pair aloud. Notice the devoicing in the singular or base form.

sections.heading: Up next
sections.body: Lesson 1.6 covers vowel length — the distinction between Mann and Bahn, Bett and Beet. After that, consonant clusters (sch, pf, qu, tz), and then you will read your first full German sentences.

lesson_completion.criteria: Mark complete when you can pronounce ten German words with final devoicing automatically, without thinking about the rule.
